processing: A clone, not a processing style: plants are grown from cuttings and the leaf is made in the Darjeeling way, mostly as black tea, lightly oxidised in spring and fuller in summer.
harvest_season: Across the Darjeeling flushes, with one estate describing distinct spring, summer and autumn characters.
appearance_dry: As is typical of Darjeeling clonal lots, twisted leaf in green and brown, darker later in the year.
appearance_liquor: Typically pale gold in spring and amber in summer, as with other Darjeeling.
appearance_wet: Typically green with coppery edges in spring, more copper later.
taste_profile: By one estate's account, floral with citrus and light honey in spring; chocolate, toffee, berries and muscatel in summer; and chocolate, berries and a forest note in autumn.

brewing.notes: Usual Darjeeling Western-style start; shorter and cooler for spring lots, and hotter water for summer and autumn.

vintage_note: Sold by estate, flush and harvest year, with the clone named on some single-garden lots. As with other Darjeeling, spring lots are for drinking young, while summer and autumn lots keep somewhat longer.
description:
P312 is one of the clones behind newer Darjeeling plantings, named alongside B157 and AV2. One estate that grows it presents it as its floral clone.

Like other clones it is grown from cuttings of one selected bush, which keeps the field uniform, and processing follows normal Darjeeling practice. The name appears on estate lots more than on shop shelves.

Gopaldhara, which grows it, describes spring tea with florals, citrus and mild honey, then chocolate, toffee, berries and a muscatel twist in summer, and chocolate and forest notes in autumn. That is one garden's account, but it does show how far a single clone can travel through a year. Brew gently in spring and more firmly later.

Buy it by estate, flush and year, and treat the clone name as a clue rather than a guarantee. It has also been noted for resistance to blister blight, which interests growers more than drinkers.
history: P312 is documented as one of the cultivars used for newer plantings adapted to Darjeeling. The name seems to refer to the Phoobsering garden, but a reliable account of who selected it and when is hard to find, so its origin remains largely unrecorded for the general reader.
